title: The Star We Almost Missed
sub: One of our closest neighbours, found in 2003
blurb: Twelve and a half light-years away, in the horns of Aries, sits one of the nearest stars to the Sun. It is so faint that generations of sky surveys passed straight over it, and it carried no name at all until 2003 — long after almost every other star in our neighbourhood had been catalogued.

title: Found in Old Data
blurb: It was not discovered by pointing a telescope at it. A team led by Bonnard Teegarden trawled back through archived images taken to track near-Earth asteroids, hunting for anything that shifted between frames. One faint dot moved far too fast to be distant. It had been sitting in that data for years.

title: Barely Wider Than Jupiter
sub: A hundred Jupiters in one Jupiter's skin
blurb: Teegarden's Star holds roughly nine per cent of the Sun's mass inside about eleven per cent of its width — around a hundred Jupiters crushed into a ball only a few per cent wider than Jupiter itself. A little less mass and its core would never have grown hot enough to fuse hydrogen at all.

title: A Thousand Times Fainter
blurb: Its surface sits near 2,900 K — cool enough that the light it does give off is mostly infrared, invisible to us. In visible light it shines with under a thousandth of the Sun's output. That is why a star this close stayed hidden for so long: proximity counts for nothing when there is almost nothing to see.

title: Older Than the Sun
sub: Alight for about eight billion years
blurb: Estimates put Teegarden's Star at roughly eight billion years old — already ancient when the Sun and Earth formed. And it has barely begun: a red dwarf this small burns its fuel so slowly that it will still be shining long after every star you can see tonight has died.

title: Three Small Worlds
sub: Not a gas giant among them
blurb: Two planets were announced in 2019 and a third followed in 2024. Every one of them weighs about as much as Earth or a little less — an unusually tidy system of small rocky worlds, with nothing resembling Jupiter or Neptune found anywhere in it.

title: The Closest Match to Home
blurb: Astronomers rank worlds against Earth on a scale from 0 to 1 called the Earth Similarity Index, weighing size, density and temperature. Teegarden b came in at 0.95 — the highest any known planet has scored. It is a measure of resemblance, not of life, but nothing else has come closer.

title: A Year in Under Five Days
sub: The whole system fits inside Mercury's orbit
blurb: The innermost world laps its star every 4.9 days; the outermost takes 26. Even the widest of the three orbits sits at under a tenth of the Earth–Sun distance — the entire system would disappear inside Mercury's orbit with room to spare. Around a star this cool, that is simply where the warmth is.

title: They Could See Us
sub: From there, Earth crosses the Sun
blurb: Almost every planet we know was found by watching a star dim as a world passed in front of it — a trick that only works from the right angle. Teegarden's Star happens to lie in that narrow band for us. An observer there, watching our Sun, would see Earth cross its face and could find us exactly as we found them.

title: Twelve and a Half Light-Years
sub: Close enough to be a neighbour
blurb: At 12.5 light-years, Teegarden's Star is among the couple of dozen nearest systems to the Sun. Light leaving it now reaches us in the middle of the next decade — near enough that the next generation of telescopes may be able to sniff the air of its worlds directly.
